Hi all — we're seeing degraded performance with search right now. Some queries are returning slowly or timing out, and results may be incomplete. The rest of the product is unaffected.

Our engineering team is actively investigating and working on a fix. If customers reach out about slow or missing search results, you can let them know we're aware of the issue and working to resolve it as quickly as possible. No action is needed on their end.

I'll post updates in this thread as we learn more, and I'll confirm here once things are back to normal.

If you want to add a status page link or a specific ETA once you have one, drop it into the second paragraph.

```
Upgrade Postgres driver from 3.1 to 4.0

Bumps the Postgres driver to 4.0 to pick up the latest bug fixes and
performance improvements.

4.0 is a major release, so note the following changes:
- Connection pool options moved under a `pool` config object
- Query results now return typed values instead of strings for
  numeric and date columns
- Deprecated callback-style APIs have been removed

Updated call sites and connection setup accordingly. Test suite passes
against Postgres 14 and 16.
```

You'll want to adjust the bullet points to match the actual breaking changes you hit — I've filled in the kinds of things a major driver bump usually involves. If the upgrade was purely mechanical with no code changes, the first paragraph plus a link to the changelog is plenty.
Thank you so much for covering my on-call shift — I really appreciate you stepping in, especially on short notice. Let me know when you need a shift covered and I'll return the favor.

Here are a few options depending on how much room you have.

**Short (single line):**
> Archive this project to hide it from your active list. Nothing is deleted, and you can restore it anytime.

**Slightly longer, with the consequences spelled out:**
> Archiving moves this project out of your active list and makes it read-only. Its data, files, and history are preserved, and members keep access. You can restore it at any time from Archived projects.

**Very short, for a compact tooltip:**
> Hide this project without deleting it. Restore anytime.

The main things worth communicating are that archiving is reversible, that nothing is lost, and where the project goes. If archiving in your product also does something less obvious — like stopping notifications, freeing up a seat, or pausing billing — add that, since it's the part people are most likely to be surprised by.

**Deciding our mobile release cadence — 30 minutes**

*Goal: leave the meeting with a decided cadence and an owner for rolling it out.*

**1. Context and constraints (5 min)**
Quick recap of how we ship today, current pain points, and any hard constraints — app store review times, QA capacity, the release checklist, upcoming launches.

**2. The options on the table (5 min)**
Brief walkthrough of the candidates, e.g. weekly, biweekly, monthly, or continuous with feature flags. One or two lines each, no debate yet.

**3. Discussion (12 min)**
What each option costs us and buys us: QA and release-engineering load, how fast fixes reach users, how much batching risk we take on, what it means for the on-call and support teams.

**4. Decide (5 min)**
Pick one. If we can't agree, pick a default to trial for one quarter and name what would make us change it.

**5. Next steps (3 min)**
Owner, first release date under the new cadence, and what needs to change in tooling or process before then.

**Before the meeting:** please skim the last quarter's release history (link) so we're not spending time reconstructing it in the room.

**Attendees:** keep it to people who can actually make the call — eng lead, mobile leads for iOS and Android, QA, product.

A couple of notes: keep the specific compliment genuine and concrete, since a vague one reads worse than none at all. And only offer feedback or a future reach-out if you actually intend to follow through.

```markdown
# seedy

A CLI for seeding test data into local and staging environments.

`seedy` creates realistic, related records — users, orgs, projects, and
the associations between them — so you can work against a database that
looks like production without copying production data. It's meant for
local development, integration tests, and demo environments.

## Quick start

```bash
# Install
brew install internal/tap/seedy

# Seed a small dataset into your local database
seedy apply --profile small

# Wipe everything seedy created and start over
seedy reset
```

## What it does

- Generates deterministic fake data from a seed value, so the same
  command produces the same dataset every time
- Respects foreign keys and creates records in dependency order
- Ships with named profiles (`small`, `medium`, `enterprise`) that
  represent common account shapes
- Tags everything it creates so `seedy reset` can clean up without
  touching data you added by hand

## What it doesn't do

- It will not run against production. Connections to hosts on the
  production allowlist are refused.
- It doesn't migrate schemas. Run your migrations first.
```

Swap in the real tool name, install method, and profile names. The "what it doesn't do" section is worth keeping — for an internal tool, the fastest way to save yourself support questions is to state the boundaries up front.

**Migration status — [Date]**

The migration is currently about two weeks behind our original schedule, with a revised completion target of [new date]. The delay came primarily from [cause — e.g., unexpected data inconsistencies in the legacy records, which required us to build and run a reconciliation pass before we could cut over safely]. The work itself is progressing: [X of Y] services are now migrated and running on the new system, and the remaining ones are smaller and better understood than the ones we've already completed. To protect the revised date, we've [mitigation — e.g., pulled two engineers off the roadmap work for the next sprint and deferred the non-critical reporting endpoints to a follow-on phase]. No customer-facing impact so far, and we don't anticipate any. I'll flag immediately if the new date comes under threat; otherwise the next update will be [date].

A few notes on the structure: lead with the number and the new date rather than building up to it, name the cause without over-explaining it, show that the trend is good if it is, and say what you're doing about it. The last line matters more than people expect — committing to a next update is what stops leadership from checking in daily.

A one-in-five failure rate is actually good news — it's frequent enough that you can reproduce it without heroics. Here's roughly the order I'd work in.

**First, get data instead of anecdotes.** Make CI record every failure: which test, which shard, which machine, what time, and the full output. If your CI doesn't already aggregate this, even a simple log of failures into a spreadsheet will do at first. You're looking for whether it's one test failing repeatedly, a cluster of related tests, or genuinely scattered failures — those three point in very different directions.

**Then reproduce it in a loop.** Run the suspect test (or the whole suite) a few hundred times locally or on a dedicated CI job:

```bash
for i in $(seq 1 200); do
  pytest tests/test_thing.py -x || echo "FAILED on run $i"
done
```

If it fails in isolation, the test itself is flaky. If it only fails as part of the full suite, it's an interaction problem, which is far more common.

**The usual suspects, in rough order of likelihood:**

- **Test order dependence.** Tests leak state — a global, a cached singleton, a database row that wasn't rolled back, a monkeypatch that wasn't undone. Most runners can shuffle test order (`pytest -p randomly`, `--random-order`, Jest's `--randomize`). If shuffling makes failures more frequent, this is your answer. Then bisect: run the failing test with progressively smaller subsets of the tests that preceded it until you find the poisoner.
- **Time.** Tests that assume "now" behaves nicely: timezone boundaries, DST, tests that break at midnight, timestamps compared with `==`, or assumptions that two `now()` calls return the same value. Freeze the clock.
- **Concurrency.** Real race conditions in the code under test, or tests that share a resource (the same database, the same port, the same temp file) when running in parallel. Try running with parallelism disabled — if the flakiness disappears, it's isolation, not logic.
- **Sleeps and waits.** `sleep(0.5)` and then asserting something finished. These fail whenever CI is loaded. Replace with polling on the actual condition with a generous timeout.
- **Unseeded randomness.** Random data generators that occasionally produce an edge case the code genuinely doesn't handle. Log the seed on every run so a failure is reproducible.
- **External dependencies.** Network calls, real DNS, a shared staging service. Stub them.

**A few practical habits that help:**

Quarantine aggressively. Move known-flaky tests to a separate job that doesn't block merges, but track them and give them owners — a quarantine with no exit path just becomes a graveyard. Fix the flake rather than adding retries; retries are fine as a short-term shield, but they hide real race conditions in your product code, which is the failure mode you actually care about. And when you find a cause, ask whether it's a class of problem rather than one test — usually the same shared-state pattern exists in a dozen places.

One more thing worth saying: a meaningful fraction of "flaky tests" turn out to be genuine, rare bugs in the system under test. Don't assume the test is wrong.

Fix CI. Almost certainly, and it isn't close.

Splitting the monorepo doesn't actually make your builds faster — it just makes them invisible to each other. You still run the same total work; you've just hidden it behind repo boundaries and traded a slow CI for a distributed-systems problem in your development process: cross-repo version bumps, dependency drift, changes that now require three coordinated PRs, and the loss of atomic refactors right at the size where those are most valuable. Teams that split at 40 engineers often spend the next year building the tooling that recreates what the monorepo gave them for free.

Also worth naming: 30 minutes of CI is annoying but it isn't a crisis. It's roughly the point at which people stop context-switching cleanly, so it's worth attacking, but it's a normal engineering problem with normal engineering fixes.

**Where the time usually goes.** Before optimizing anything, instrument the pipeline and find out. In my experience, the answer is one of a small number of things:

- **You're testing everything on every change.** This is the big one. Build a dependency graph and run only what a change can actually affect. Bazel, Nx, Turborepo, and Pants all do this; so does a modest homegrown script if your dependency structure is simple. For most monorepos this alone cuts the median PR build by more than half, because most PRs touch one corner.
- **Nothing is cached.** Dependency installs, compilation artifacts, Docker layers. A remote build cache shared across CI and developer machines is often the single highest-leverage change.
- **Insufficient parallelism.** Slow tests running sequentially on a small machine. Sharding tests across more runners is mostly a money problem, and runner time is far cheaper than engineer time. Do the arithmetic on 40 engineers waiting — it makes the budget conversation easy.
- **A long tail of slow tests.** Usually a handful of integration tests dominate. Find the slowest 20 and either speed them up or move them off the blocking path.
- **Serialized stages.** Lint, then build, then test, then package, each waiting on the last. Much of that can run concurrently.

**Reframe the target, too.** The number that matters isn't total pipeline time, it's time-to-signal on a PR: how long until a developer learns their change is broken. Run the fast, high-value checks first and fail immediately. Push slow, rarely-failing suites (full end-to-end, cross-browser, performance) to a post-merge or scheduled run. Not every check needs to block every merge.

**When splitting would actually be the answer:** if you have genuinely independent products with no shared code and separate release cycles, or a component with wildly different tooling or compliance requirements, or an open-source piece that can't live alongside proprietary code. Those are structural reasons, not performance reasons. "CI is slow" is not on that list.

If I were you, I'd spend two weeks on build instrumentation plus affected-target selection plus caching, and I'd expect to land somewhere under ten minutes. If after that you're still at 30 minutes, come back to the question — but you'll be asking it with much better data.

Idempotency means: doing the same operation twice has the same effect as doing it once.

You already use idempotent operations without calling them that. `GET /users/42` is idempotent — fetching it ten times doesn't change anything. So is `DELETE /users/42`: the first call deletes the user, and the next nine find nothing to delete and leave the world in the same state. `PUT /users/42` with a full body is idempotent too, because you're setting the record to a specific value rather than nudging it.

The one that isn't is `POST /orders`. Call it twice, get two orders.

**Why anyone cares.** Networks lie. A client sends a request, the server processes it successfully, and the response is lost on the way back. From the client's point of view, this looks identical to the request never arriving. So the client retries — and now you have two orders, or two charges, or two emails.

This isn't a rare edge case. It happens with mobile clients on flaky connections, with load balancer timeouts, with retry logic in HTTP libraries you didn't know was enabled, and with message queues that guarantee at-least-once delivery. Any system with retries anywhere in it will eventually deliver you a duplicate.

**How you make a non-idempotent operation safe.** The standard approach is an idempotency key. The client generates a unique ID for the operation — a UUID it creates once and reuses across retries — and sends it along:

```
POST /orders
Idempotency-Key: 7c9e6679-7425-40de-944b-e07fc1f90ae7

{"item_id": 123, "quantity": 2}
```

On the server:

1. Look up the key. If you've seen it and the operation completed, return the stored response and do nothing else.
2. If you haven't seen it, record it, do the work, store the response against the key, and return it.

Steps 1 and 2 need to be atomic, or two concurrent retries can both pass the check. A unique constraint on the key column is the simplest way to get this: try to insert, and if you get a duplicate-key error, you know someone else got there first. Keys typically expire after a day or so.

This is exactly what Stripe does, and it's worth reading their API docs on it — the pattern is well worn.

**Two things that trip people up.**

First, idempotent isn't the same as "returns the same response." A second `DELETE` might legitimately return 404 instead of 204. What matters is that the *state* of the system is the same, not that the bytes coming back are identical. (Though returning the stored original response is usually kinder to clients.)

Second, watch out for operations that look idempotent but aren't. `UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100` is not idempotent — run it twice and you've taken 200. `UPDATE accounts SET balance = 400` is. Relative changes are the danger; absolute assignments are safe.

**The practical rule:** if an operation creates something, charges something, sends something, or increments something, assume a duplicate will arrive one day and design for it. Everything else you probably get for free.

The honest answer is that it depends on things specific to your situation, but there's a way to think about it that usually makes the choice fall out.

**Start with what's actually blocking you.** Two juniors give you more total hours. One senior gives you more judgment. If your bottleneck is throughput on well-understood work — there's a clear backlog, someone knows how each piece should be done, the patterns are established — juniors add real capacity. If your bottleneck is that nobody knows how to do the thing, or that decisions keep getting made badly, or that you're the only person who can be trusted with the hard problems, more hands don't help. You need another brain.

**Then be honest about your capacity to absorb juniors.** This is the part people underestimate. Two juniors is not a neutral addition — it's a commitment to mentorship, code review, pairing, unblocking, and a certain amount of rework. For the first three to six months, they will probably consume more senior time than they produce in output. That's fine and expected, but it means the real question isn't "senior or juniors," it's "do I have senior capacity to spare?" If your existing seniors are already at capacity and slightly underwater, hiring two juniors makes things worse before it makes them better. A team with a healthy senior bench and someone who genuinely enjoys mentoring can absorb them easily.

**Consider the team's shape, not just its size.** If you have five seniors and no juniors, you probably have people doing work that's beneath them, and everything gets gold-plated. If you have five juniors and one senior, that senior is a bottleneck and will burn out. Hire toward balance.

**A few situational tiebreakers:**

- **Small team (under ~8) with no slack:** lean senior. Small teams can't carry a ramp-up period, and a generalist who can cover multiple areas is disproportionately valuable.
- **You need a specific capability you don't have** — mobile, infra, ML, security: senior, clearly. You can't grow it from someone who's never seen it.
- **You're planning to grow a lot over the next two years:** juniors are a better long-term investment, and the seniors you hire now become the people who train them. But that only works if you actually retain them — junior hiring pays off on a two-to-three-year horizon, so if your retention is poor, you're training for someone else.
- **The work is genuinely well-understood and there's a lot of it:** juniors.
- **Your senior is a single point of failure on something important:** senior, for the bus-factor reason alone.

**Two practical cautions.** One, "two juniors for the price of one senior" often isn't true once you count recruiting, onboarding, equipment, and management overhead — and it's definitely not true in the first year. Two, a senior generalist is only worth it if you actually hire a good one; a mediocre senior is worse than two eager juniors, because they cost more and are harder to move on from. If the market or your pipeline means you'd be settling, the juniors look better.

**If I had to give a default:** for most teams in the 5-15 person range with a real backlog and stretched senior capacity, one senior generalist. The leverage of someone who can work independently, make good calls without supervision, and raise the level of the people around them tends to beat raw headcount. Flip to juniors when you have genuine mentorship bandwidth and a multi-year horizon.

Don't fight the request, and don't deliver the number as asked. Both of those are losing moves — refusing makes you look defensive and like you have something to hide, and handing over a single number means it becomes a target, gets gamed within a quarter, and eventually gets used in a way you'll regret.

**Figure out what they actually want first.** "A number for engineering productivity" is almost never the real ask. Underneath it there's usually something concrete: they're deciding whether to add headcount, they've heard a complaint that engineering is slow, they need something to say to the board, they suspect a specific team is struggling, or they want to know if a big investment paid off. Ask directly: "What decision are you trying to make with it?" A specific question has a specific answer, and it's usually a better one than a productivity index.

**Explain the failure mode briefly, without lecturing.** One or two sentences is enough. Something like: "Any single number here becomes the thing people optimize — if we measure PRs merged, we'll get more, smaller PRs, not more value delivered. I'd rather give you something that stays honest." Most leaders have seen enough Goodhart's-law situations to nod along. Don't spend ten minutes on it; you'll sound like you're dodging.

**Then counter-offer with something real.** The strongest move is to show up with an alternative rather than an objection. A few options depending on what they're after:

*If they want to know whether engineering is healthy and improving,* the DORA metrics are the standard answer and they're defensible because they're industry-benchmarked: deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate, and time to restore service. Four numbers, they trade off against each other so gaming one shows up in another, and they measure the system rather than individuals.

*If they want to know where the effort is going,* show investment allocation: roughly what percentage of engineering time went to new product work, maintenance, reliability, and platform. This is often what leadership is really asking, and it's a genuinely useful conversation.

*If they want to know whether engineering is delivering,* tie it to outcomes: what shipped this quarter, what it moved. This is the least gameable framing because it's about the business, not the activity.

*If they want a dashboard-friendly single line,* the closest defensible thing is lead time — commit to production — because shortening it requires actually fixing the system: testing, review latency, deploy pipeline, batch size. It's the one number I'd be least unhappy about. Pair it with change failure rate so speed can't be bought with quality.

**Two hard lines worth holding.** Never let it be per-engineer. Individual metrics — lines of code, commits, story points, PR counts — destroy collaboration, punish the people doing the hard and unglamorous work, and are trivially gamed. And never report on something you can't explain the movement in; you'll get asked "why did it go down" and "I don't know" is worse than not having reported it.

**How to run the conversation.** Go in with a one-page proposal rather than an argument. Say yes to the underlying need, name what you'll report and how often, and be clear about what it can and can't tell them. Something like: "Here are four numbers I'll report monthly, here's what each one means, here's what would make me worried, and here's what I'd want us to *not* do with them." That reads as taking the request seriously, which is what they wanted in the first place.

If they insist on the single number anyway after all that — give them lead time, write down the caveats, and revisit in two quarters. It's not worth burning capital over, and a well-chosen mediocre metric is survivable.

The fear is usually rational — it means the module has no safety net and everyone knows it. The way out isn't to be braver, it's to build the net first. Rewriting it before you understand it is how these situations get worse.

**Step one: understand it before touching it.** Spend real time reading it and write down what you learn — a short document describing what it's responsible for, who calls it, what it calls, and what the non-obvious behaviors are. If nobody currently understands the module, no amount of test coverage will save you, because you won't know what the tests should assert. Find whoever has touched it most recently and get an hour of their time. Check the git history and the issue tracker for the bugs it has caused; those tell you where the sharp edges are.

**Step two: find out what it actually does in production.** The documented behavior and the real behavior are different, and the difference is where the fear lives. Add logging or tracing around its entry points and let it run for a week. Capture real inputs. You'll usually find cases nobody knew about — a caller passing nulls, a legacy format still in use, a code path that fires once a month at billing time.

**Step three: pin the current behavior with tests, bugs included.** This is the core of it. Write characterization tests: tests that assert what the code does today, not what it should do. If the module returns an empty string on a certain input, assert the empty string, even if that's clearly wrong. You're not documenting correctness, you're building a tripwire so you can tell when you've changed behavior. Note the ones you believe are bugs so you can fix them deliberately later, as separate changes.

Where the module is hard to test because of tangled dependencies, resist the urge to restructure it first. Use whatever seam you can get cheaply — a wrapper, an integration test that goes through the database, a golden-file test that captures the whole output. Michael Feathers' *Working Effectively with Legacy Code* is essentially a catalog of techniques for exactly this problem, and it's worth having on the shelf.

If the module transforms data, the highest-leverage test you can write is often a snapshot test: feed it a large set of real production inputs, record every output, and store them. That single test catches almost every accidental behavior change and takes an afternoon.

**Step four: change it in small, boring, reversible steps.** Once you have coverage, the refactoring itself should be dull. Extract one function. Run the tests. Commit. Rename one thing. Run the tests. Commit. Resist the big-bang rewrite — long-lived refactor branches on scary modules are where projects go to die, because they can't be merged and can't be verified.

For anything genuinely risky, run the old and new paths in parallel and compare. Send real traffic through both, log every disagreement, fix the disagreements, and only then switch over. GitHub's Scientist library popularized this pattern, and there are ports for most languages. It converts "we think it's equivalent" into evidence.

**Step five: make it stay safe.** Once you can change it, close the loop: keep the characterization tests, add the documentation you wrote at the start to the repo, and make sure at least two people have now worked in it. A lot of the fear around these modules is really fear of being the only person who touched it last.

**One practical note on scope.** Don't try to fix the whole module. Pick the part you actually need to change and make *that* part safe. The rest can stay scary until someone needs it. A six-month project to clean up a module nobody was asked to clean up will get cancelled halfway through and leave things in a worse state than when you started.

A preflight failure is your browser telling you: *I asked the server for permission to send this request, and the server didn't grant it.* Importantly, it's the browser blocking you, not the server rejecting you. The server may well be perfectly happy to serve the request.

**What preflight actually is.** For requests that could have side effects, the browser doesn't just send them and hope. Before your actual request goes out, it sends an `OPTIONS` request to the same URL asking, essentially, "am I allowed to send a PUT to this endpoint, from this origin, with a `Content-Type: application/json` header?" That's the preflight. The server answers with `Access-Control-Allow-*` headers. If the answer doesn't cover what you're about to do, the browser cancels the real request and you get the error.

Preflight is triggered when your request isn't "simple" — in practice that means anything other than GET/HEAD/POST, or a POST with a content type other than form-encoded, multipart, or plain text, or any request with custom headers. Sending JSON with `Content-Type: application/json` triggers it, which is why nearly every modern API hits this.

**Reading the specific failure.** The browser's message usually names the exact clause that failed, and it's worth reading it carefully rather than pattern-matching to "CORS problem":

- *"No 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header is present"* — the OPTIONS response didn't include the header at all. Often this means the OPTIONS request never reached your CORS middleware: a router that only handles GET/POST, an auth layer rejecting the unauthenticated OPTIONS with a 401, or a proxy swallowing it.
- *"Origin ... is not allowed"* — the header was there but didn't match. Check for exact string equality: scheme, host, and port all count, and a trailing slash breaks it. `http://localhost:3000` and `https://localhost:3000` are different origins.
- *"Method PUT is not allowed by Access-Control-Allow-Methods"* — self-explanatory; add the method.
- *"Request header field authorization is not allowed by Access-Control-Allow-Headers"* — every non-standard request header you send has to be listed. Custom headers like `X-Request-Id` are the usual culprit.
- *"The value of 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' must not be the wildcard when credentials mode is 'include'"* — you can't combine `*` with cookies. You must echo back the specific origin and also send `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`.
- *"Response to preflight request doesn't pass access control check: It does not have HTTP ok status"* — your OPTIONS handler returned a 4xx or 5xx. It needs to return 200 or 204.

**The debugging move that saves the most time:** open the network tab, find the `OPTIONS` request specifically (not the one you meant to send), and look at its response headers. Everything you need is there. Then reproduce the same request with curl:

```bash
curl -i -X OPTIONS https://api.example.com/things \
  -H "Origin: https://app.example.com" \
  -H "Access-Control-Request-Method: PUT" \
  -H "Access-Control-Request-Headers: content-type,authorization"
```

If curl shows the right headers coming back and the browser still fails, something between you and the server — a CDN, load balancer, or service worker — is altering the response.

**Two things worth internalizing.** First, CORS is not a security mechanism protecting your server. It protects *users* from having their browser silently make authenticated requests to other sites on a malicious page's behalf. Your server is still fully reachable by curl, mobile apps, and anything else that isn't a browser, so disabling CORS checks doesn't expose anything that wasn't already exposed — but it does remove a protection your users benefit from. Set the allowed origins correctly rather than reflexively wildcarding.

Second, if you're seeing this in local development against a production-ish API and you control neither side's CORS config, a dev-server proxy is usually the right answer — it makes the request same-origin and the whole problem disappears.

A healthy p50 with a terrible p99 tells you the system is fundamentally fast and something is intermittently getting in the way. That's a different problem from "everything is slow," and it narrows the search a lot. You're hunting for something that affects a small fraction of requests, badly.

**Before anything else: get per-request tracing.** Averages and percentiles tell you that a problem exists; they can't tell you where. You need to be able to pull up individual slow requests and see the breakdown. If you have distributed tracing, sample the tail specifically — most tracing setups sample randomly, which means they capture almost none of the requests you care about. Tail-based sampling, or just logging a full timing breakdown for any request over some threshold, is the single highest-leverage thing here.

Then ask the first branching question: **are the slow requests a particular kind of request, or are they random?**

**If they cluster on specific endpoints or specific users,** it's usually data-dependent work. The classic shapes:

- A query that's fine for the average account and catastrophic for your largest one. Pagination that works until someone has 50,000 records. An N+1 query where N is normally 3 and occasionally 4,000.
- Missing index that the query planner works around fine on small partitions and not on large ones.
- Unbounded loops over user data, serialization of large response bodies, or in-memory sorting that scales with account size.

These are the easiest to fix, and they're the most common cause when p50 and p99 diverge this sharply. Check whether your slow requests correlate with account size — it's often a one-query investigation.

**If the slow requests look random,** you're looking at contention or resource limits, and the usual suspects are:

- **Connection pool exhaustion.** Requests are fast when they get a database connection and slow when they queue for one. This produces exactly your signature: fine at p50, cliff at the tail. Check pool wait time as a separate metric from query time — if you're not measuring it, you're blind to it.
- **Garbage collection pauses.** In JVM, Go, or Node, a stop-the-world pause lands on whatever unlucky requests are in flight. Plot GC pause duration against your p99; if they track, that's your answer. Same signature from any runtime-level stall.
- **Lock contention.** Database row locks, table locks during migrations, or application-level mutexes. Look for slow queries that aren't slow when run manually — that gap is usually lock wait.
- **Queueing.** If your service is running near capacity, queueing theory does the rest: utilization above roughly 70-80% makes tail latency explode even though the average looks fine. Check whether p99 correlates with request rate. If it does, you have a capacity problem masquerading as a performance problem, and the fix is more headroom, not faster code.
- **A slow dependency's tail.** If you call three services and each has a 1% slow tail, your p99 is worse than any of theirs. Fan-out amplifies tails. Check the timings of downstream calls specifically, and look at whether retries are involved — a retry after a timeout adds the full timeout to the request.
- **Cold caches and cold starts.** Cache misses are much slower than hits, so if your hit rate is 97%, your tail is made entirely of misses. Same for serverless cold starts, JIT warm-up, and lazily-initialized connections.
- **One bad host.** In a fleet, a single degraded instance — failing disk, noisy neighbor, stuck in a bad state — can own most of your tail. Break your p99 down by instance. If one host is responsible, you've got your answer in five minutes.

**A practical order of attack.** Break p99 down by endpoint, then by host, then by customer. One of those three dimensions usually isolates it immediately, and each one takes minutes. If none of them do, look at connection pool wait time and GC pauses next. If it's still diffuse, plot p99 against request rate and check whether you're simply running hot.

**One thing to be careful about:** make sure your p99 is measured at the right place. Measured inside the application, it excludes time spent queueing at the load balancer, in the accept queue, or in TLS handshakes — which for tail latency is often where the time actually goes. If your server-side p99 is 200ms and the client sees 4 seconds, stop looking at the application entirely and look at what's in front of it.
